patch.title: Wasserstein Bought New York Magazine After a Bid Led by Zuckerman and Wolff
patch.description_medium: In December 2003, Bruce Wasserstein agreed to buy New York Magazine from Primedia for $55 million, beating a competing consortium assembled by Mort Zuckerman and Michael Wolff. The group included financier Jeffrey Epstein, according to contemporaneous and later reporting. Wasserstein formed New York Media Holdings for the purchase, which was expected to close within 30 days. The available reporting does not connect Donald Trump to the sale or to the competing bid.
patch.description_long:
Primedia put New York Magazine up for sale in 2003 as it sold titles to reduce debt. Bruce Wasserstein won the auction with a $55 million offer, announced on December 16. A competing group led by New York Daily News owner Mort Zuckerman and media columnist Michael Wolff had assembled investors that included Jeffrey Epstein, Harvey Weinstein, advertising executive Donny Deutsch and other wealthy figures. The Washington Post reported Wasserstein’s successful offer and the auction’s other bidders; the New York Observer’s contemporaneous coverage described Zuckerman’s group learning that Primedia had agreed to sell to Wasserstein. Later reporting also identified Epstein as among its backers.

Wasserstein created New York Media Holdings to acquire the magazine, then a 35-year-old weekly with a reported average circulation of about 425,000. The deal was a media-industry contest between investor groups, not a documented Trump transaction. The linked and corroborating accounts do not place Donald Trump among the bidders or show that he influenced which group prevailed.
patch.evidence_notes: The Washington Post confirms Wasserstein’s $55 million purchase; contemporaneous Observer coverage and later Guardian reporting identify the Zuckerman-Wolff consortium and Epstein among its backers. None connects Trump to the sale.

reason: Contemporaneous and later reporting supports the Epstein/Wolff/Zuckerman consortium; the first draft incorrectly omitted their attempted bid.

patch.description_long:
Brett Kavanaugh’s 2006 appointment to the federal appeals court was part of President George W. Bush’s judicial nominations. The Senate roll-call record shows that on May 26, 2006, it voted to confirm Kavanaugh as a judge of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. The White House archive describes the D.C. Circuit’s role in hearing appeals from the federal district court in Washington and reviewing decisions by federal agencies. Kavanaugh served on that court before President Donald Trump nominated him to the Supreme Court in 2018, a separate confirmation process.

The records for this 2006 event establish the appointment, but do not identify testimony that was false or evidence supporting a claim that Kavanaugh lied under oath. Trump’s later Supreme Court nomination was a separate event. The available confirmation record therefore supports an account of Kavanaugh’s appellate appointment, not the accusation in the original title.

reason: Replaces editor-directed language with a reader-facing account of the source-supported 2006 appointment and the unsupported perjury claim.

patch.description_medium: In a telephone interview published in New York Magazine’s October 2002 profile of Jeffrey Epstein, Donald Trump said he had known Epstein for about 15 years and called him a “terrific guy” and “a lot of fun to be with.” Trump also said Epstein liked beautiful women, “many of them on the younger side.” The remarks documented their social acquaintance at the time; they do not establish what Trump knew about Epstein’s later criminal conduct.

reason: Removes the mistaken implication that Trump repeated Epstein’s own remark; the profile attributes the description to Trump.
